items.title: Effects of AI-Supported Learning on Independent Cognitive Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Instructional Scaffolding and Learner Characteristics
items.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis will examine the effects of AI-supported learning on objectively assessed cognitive performance when AI assistance is unavailable during assessment. It will cover intelligent tutoring systems, traditional chatbots, adaptive learning platforms, and generative AI across educational stages and subject areas. Technology characteristics and instructional support functions will be coded separately, allowing overlapping features rather than imposing mutually exclusive technology categories. The primary objective is to estimate the effects of AI-supported learning compared with non-AI learning conditions on independent cognitive performance. Secondary objectives are to examine direct comparisons between AI-supported instructional approaches and whether effects vary with baseline learner characteristics and instructional support functions. Relevant support functions include hints, explanations, feedback, worked examples, self-explanation prompts, verification and revision prompts, adaptive learning pathways, and restrictions or fading of AI assistance. Randomized and non-randomized controlled intervention studies will be synthesized separately. A distinct observational evidence stream will examine associations between actual AI use, such as usage frequency, help-seeking, and verification behaviors, and eligible cognitive outcomes. These associations will not be combined with intervention effects or interpreted as causal evidence that a particular use behavior improves learning. Eligible outcomes include objective measures of knowledge and understanding, application and transfer, other cognitive skills, and composite achievement, which will be analyzed separately. The first eligible post-intervention assessment and subsequent delayed assessments will be distinguished. Assessments must be completed without AI; access to non-AI resources will be recorded separately. Unclear AI permissions will remain awaiting clarification rather than being treated as confirmed eligibility or grounds for automatic exclusion. Two human reviewers will independently screen records, extract key study information, and assess risk of bias, with disagreements reconciled. Analyses will account for overlapping reports, shared samples, dependent effect sizes, and differences in study design and comparison conditions. Moderator analyses will depend on sufficient comparable evidence. Within-study learner moderation will be distinguished from between-study associations. The review aims to clarify whether benefits of AI-supported learning persist when learners are assessed without AI, and which learner characteristics and instructional support functions may be associated with those benefits. No uniformly positive effect or ranking of technologies is assumed. Before registration, preliminary scoping and pilot screening examined 30 purposively selected candidate reports, and selected results from four reports underwent trial extraction to assess feasibility and refine the protocol. This prior exposure to study findings is disclosed. A comprehensive systematic database search, formal independent duplicate screening, complete data extraction, and quantitative synthesis have not yet been conducted. Substantive subsequent changes will be documented through dated amendments.

items.title: Enhancing network science with large language models and federated artificial intelligence
items.abstract: Abstract Sixth generation (6G) networks require intelligent and privacy-preserving solutions to handle traffic complexity, resource allocation, and security challenges. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer advanced reasoning and Federated Artificial Intelligence (FAI) enables distributed learning without directly sharing raw data, their combined application in large-scale network science remains limited. Key issues include non-IID data, decision latency, and limited robustness of centralized models. To address these challenges, this work introduces FALCON-6G (Federated AI and LLM-Oriented Cognitive Optimization in 6G Networks), a novel framework for distributed anomaly detection, traffic prediction, and adaptive resource management. Experiments conducted under federated learning settings with 50 participating clients and 200 global communication rounds on two Open RAN and four intrusion detection datasets show a 22.7% average relative improvement in throughput prediction accuracy and a 17.6% reduction in decision latency compared with FedAvg, along with up to a 23.9% relative improvement in intrusion detection F1-score over FedAvg and a 34.0% reduction in communication overhead. These results demonstrate the potential of FALCON-6G for privacy-aware 6G network optimization. The current evaluation is primarily based on benchmark datasets, and validation in live large-scale 6G/O-RAN environments remains an important direction for future work.

items.title: ETSAM: effectively segmenting cell membranes in cryo-electron tomograms
items.abstract: Cryogenic Electron Tomography (cryo-ET) is an emerging experimental technique used to visualize cell structures and macromolecules in their native cellular environment. Accurate segmentation of cell structures in cryo-ET tomograms, such as cell membranes, supports the study of cellular organization and function. However, several inherent limitations in cryo-ET, including the very low signal-to-noise ratio, missing wedge artifacts from limited tilt angles, and other noise artifacts, collectively hinder the reliable identification and delineation of these structures. In this study, we present ETSAM, a two-stage Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2)-based fine-tuned AI method that effectively segments cell membranes in tomograms. It is trained on a diverse dataset comprising 83 experimental tomograms from the CryoET Data Portal (CDP) database and 28 simulated tomograms generated using PolNet. On an independent test set of 17 experimental tomograms for which ground-truth annotations are available, ETSAM outperforms other deep learning based methods by robustly identifying cell membranes with high sensitivity while also maintaining better precision. Cell membranes are hard to distinguish in the noisy 3D volumes from cryo-electron tomography. Here, authors adapt a video segmentation foundation model to the task, segmenting membranes across diverse organisms more accurately than existing tools.

items.title: Every Public Servant Was Once a student: Reimagining Education for Ethical Leadership, Public Service and Good Governance in Fiji and the Pacific
items.abstract: Not every student will become a public servant, but every public servant was once a student. This simple proposition raises a significant but insufficiently examined question about the wider purpose of education: to what extent does education contribute to forming the values, ethical judgement, critical consciousness and sense of public responsibility of those who later serve within public institutions? While education is frequently evaluated through academic achievement, qualifications, employability and economic productivity, comparatively less attention is given to its longer-term contribution to ethical public service and good governance. This conceptual paper critically examines the relationship between education, public-service formation and governance, with particular attention to Fiji and the wider Pacific. Drawing upon literature on democratic education, critical pedagogy, character and values education, the Capability Approach, public-service ethics and Indigenous Pacific epistemologies, the paper argues that the foundations of ethical public service begin long before an individual enters government employment. Schools, tertiary institutions, families and communities contribute to developing integrity, responsibility, empathy, critical thinking, cultural understanding, respect for diversity and commitment to the public good. These capabilities become increasingly important as public servants confront complex challenges involving inequality, climate change, digital transformation, artificial intelligence, cultural diversity and declining or contested public trust. The paper proposes an Education–Public Service–Society Cycle to conceptualise the intergenerational relationship through which education contributes to professional and civic formation; public servants subsequently influence policy implementation, institutional integrity and service delivery; and the quality of public institutions, in turn, shapes the educational and social opportunities available to future generations. In the Fiji and Pacific context, the paper further argues that ethical public-service formation should integrate professional competence with Indigenous values of relationality, collective responsibility, service and cultural accountability. It concludes that education should not merely prepare people to obtain employment in public institutions, but contribute to developing people capable of serving the public ethically, competently, equitably and with humanity. Reimagining education in this way positions the classroom as one of the earliest foundations of trustworthy institutions, responsible public administration and sustainable Pacific futures.

items.title: Exploring artificial intelligence usage preferences among medical students in Iran: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into medical education, offering opportunities to enhance learning, research, and clinical preparation. Although previous studies have explored medical students’ attitudes and acceptance of AI, evidence regarding their AI usage preferences remains limited, particularly in developing countries where AI integration into medical education is still evolving. Understanding these preferences is essential for designing context-appropriate educational strategies and responsible AI integration. This study aimed to examine the preferences and patterns of AI usage among students at Shiraz University of Medical Sciences (SUMS), Iran. This descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted in 2025 among undergraduate and postgraduate students at SUMS. Using stratified random sampling, 384 students were recruited. Data were collected between July and October 2025 using a validated self-administered questionnaire (AI-UPSS; Cronbach’s α = 0.935), assessing AI usage across eight domains. Responses were rated on a 4-point Likert scale. Data were analyzed using one-sample t-tests, independent t-tests, and one-way ANOVA in SPSS version 24, with a cutoff mean score of 2.5. The highest mean preference scores were observed in Research & Writing (Mean = 2.66 ± 0.79, p < 0.001) and Self-learning/Education (Mean = 2.61 ± 0.81, p = 0.010). Moderate preferences were found for Curiosity & Entertainment (Mean = 2.36 ± 0.81, p = 0.001) and Health Counseling (Mean = 2.40 ± 0.96, p = 0.044). The lowest scores were reported in Design & Programming (Mean = 1.54 ± 0.79, p < 0.001) and Art (Mean = 1.68 ± 0.77, p < 0.001). Significant gender differences were observed in Art ( p = 0.010), Self-learning ( p = 0.027), and Health Counseling ( p < 0.001). GPA was significantly associated with Content Development ( p = 0.004), Design & Programming ( p = 0.031), and Art ( p = 0.032), with higher usage among students with lower GPAs. Undergraduate students showed significantly higher preferences across several domains, including curiosity and health counseling ( p < 0.01). Medical students primarily use AI for academic, research, and self-directed learning purposes, while engagement with technical and creative applications remains limited. AI usage preferences are influenced by academic level, gender, and GPA rather than age or field of study. These findings underscore the need for structured, level-specific AI education to promote effective and ethical AI integration in medical curricula.

items.title: Factors Associated With Low Back Pain Complaints Among Warehouse Workers At PT. X In 2026
items.abstract: Low Back Pain (LBP) is one of the most common musculoskeletal disorders experienced by warehouse workers due to manual handling activities, non-ergonomic working postures, and repetitive physical workloads. This condition may reduce work productivity and negatively affect workers' health. This study aimed to determine the factors associated with Low Back Pain complaints among warehouse workers at PT. X in 2026. This quantitative study employed a cross-sectional design. The study population consisted of 81 warehouse workers, all of whom were included as the research sample using a total sampling technique. Data were collected using the Nordic Body Map (NBM) questionnaire to identify Low Back Pain complaints, while working posture was assessed using the Rapid Entire Body Assessment (REBA) method. Data were analyzed using univariate and bivariate analyses with the Chi-Square test at a 95% confidence level (α = 0.05). The findings indicated that most warehouse workers experienced Low Back Pain complaints. Bivariate analysis showed that age and length of employment were significantly associated with Low Back Pain complaints (p < 0.05), whereas working duration was not significantly associated with Low Back Pain (p > 0.05). The REBA assessment revealed that most work activities were classified as having moderate to high ergonomic risk, indicating the need for corrective ergonomic interventions. It can be concluded that age and length of employment are factors associated with Low Back Pain complaints among warehouse workers at PT. X. The company is recommended to implement ergonomic programs, provide manual handling aids, and conduct regular ergonomic training and working posture evaluations to reduce the risk of Low Back Pain.

items.abstract: These slides accompanied an invited tutorial presented at TCO 2026 on 28 September 2026 in Leipzig, Germany. The presentation introduces NOMAD, a free, open-source research data management platform developed and operated by FAIRmat, a consortium of the German National Research Data Infrastructure (NFDI). NOMAD enables researchers to upload, organize, explore, analyze, and publish their data. By transforming heterogeneous research data into structured, machine-readable formats, the platform helps make them findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR). The presentation provides an overview of relevant concepts, tools, and practical workflows for managing materials-science data throughout the research lifecycle. It covers data upload and automated processing, metadata extraction and enrichment, schema-based data modelling, data organization, search and exploration, analysis, and publication. It also introduces NOMAD’s support for experimental and computational data and discusses how structured, contextualized datasets can be prepared for machine-learning and artificial-intelligence applications. Both NOMAD deployment options are presented: the publicly accessible central platform and NOMAD Oasis, a customizable infrastructure that research groups and institutions can host and operate independently. The slides are intended for researchers, developers, and research-data professionals interested in interoperable data infrastructures, reproducible research, and applying the FAIR principles to computational and experimental materials science.

items.title: Fairy tales to fairer tales: Generative AI-supported critical multimodal literacy in pre-service preschool teacher education
items.abstract: This study investigates how pre-service teachers can use generative artificial intelligence (AI) to retell classic fairy tales in a way that challenges the biases that they frequently contain. A qualitative action research study involving 60 pre-service preschool teachers (46 female and 14 male) was carried out at a public university in Türkiye. Data collection included video recordings of instructional sessions (4 weeks, two lesson hours per week), participants’ fairer tales, and field notes. Drawing on the Critical Multimodal Literacy (CML) framework, the participants used generative AI tools to iteratively reimagine the textual and visual elements of traditional fairy tales. 11 reimagined fairy tales were analyzed under three themes: challenging traditional power dynamics, critiquing societal norms, and promoting non-violent conflict resolution. The findings indicate that the participants engaged in CLM by restructuring dominant representations of gender, identity, and conflict through the use of textual and visual modes. While generative AI supported the production of multimodal texts, participants maintained their agency through processes of prompting, evaluating, redesigning, and revising the outputs, emphasizing AI’s role as a mediational tool rather than an autonomous creator. The findings suggest that AI-supported fairy tale rewriting may provide a pedagogical context that enables pre-service preschool teachers to produce alternative representations of equality and social justice for children.

items.title: Fast and Accurate: Improving Personalized LLM Performance by Semantic Concentration Inspired Workload Split between RAG and Fine-Tuning
items.abstract: With ever increasing personalized large language model (LLM) services, the next question to answer is how to improve the quality of services/users' experiences, which is indicated by personalized LLM generation accuracy/quality and inference latency. Although state-of-the-art designs, e.g., parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or Full PEFT+RAG, can help, they largely ignore the heterogeneous semantic concentrations of users' historical data and cannot fully unleash the potential of personal data for personalized LLM performance enhancement. In this paper, we propose PEFT Union RAG (PUR), a novel ``fast and accurate'' approach that exploits the semantic concentration of users' personal historical data to split workload between PEFT and RAG, aiming to improve personalized LLM performance in terms of better generation accuracy/quality and lower inference latency. Briefly, PUR partitions user's personal historical data and assigns semantic concentrated ``core'' information to PEFT for offline parametric fine-tuning, while retaining dispersed information for RAG. During the online LLM inference, PUR directly generates responses for ``core'' queries covered by the PEFT region and invokes RAG only for sporadic ``peripheral'' queries. Experimental results show that, by appropriately splitting workload between PEFT and RAG, PUR consistently achieves the best generation accuracy/quality for various users across multiple tasks, while reducing inference latency by 14.4%--46.6% compared with the best performed method.

items.title: Fewer Bits, More Tries: Recovering Capability Under Memory Constraints
items.abstract: Large language models are generally more capable than smaller ones, but their memory requirements can make local deployment difficult. We ask whether part of this capability gap can instead be recovered by running a smaller or more compressed model multiple times and selecting among its outputs using public or model-generated tests. Single-user local inference can leave hardware underutilized, allowing parallel candidate generation to trade additional test-time computation for accuracy at modest latency cost. Across four code-generation benchmarks, verified retry recovers substantial accuracy lost to model size or compression. A 7B Qwen model with eight parallel attempts essentially matches a 32B model on MBPP+ and exceeds it on the other three benchmarks, while using about $4\times$ less model memory, running up to $6\times$ faster, and using less energy, as measured on Nvidia GPU. We observe similar tradeoff across model sizes, compression levels and hardware choices, although exact benefit depends on the hardware profile and problem setting. These results show that model capacity can be traded for verified test-time computation when correct solutions remain reachable within a modest retry budget.

items.title: Foundations for Investigations of Agentic AI Systems from the Forensic Analysis of OpenClaw
items.abstract: Agentic AI systems are increasingly deployed as personal assistants and virtual employees, and are likely to become a common object of digital investigations and incident response. Yet little is known about how their internal state and actions can be reconstructed during forensic analysis, and systematic forensic approaches remain largely unexplored. We present the first empirical forensic study of a personal AI assistant, with OpenClaw as a case study. We examine its technical design via static code analysis and apply differential forensic analysis to identify recoverable traces across stages of the agent interaction loop. We classify and correlate these traces, structuring the examination around representative investigative questions. We propose a five-plane agent artifact taxonomy that captures recurring investigative patterns; its structural completeness is assessed by cross-mapping against published artifact inventories of two related AI systems. To aid investigations, we release an open-source artifact-extraction tool with a machine-readable schema. Finally, we highlight a foundational challenge: LLM-mediated execution adds both an abstraction layer and substantial nondeterminism to trace generation. Because tool selection and state transitions are co-determined by the model, the execution environment, and the evolving context, identical inputs need not yield identical traces.

items.title: Framework for Screening for Professional Identity Crisis in Future Healthcare Professionals
items.abstract: Introduction. The modern system of higher medical education places increased demands on the psycholog­ical stability of students, which frequently results in a professional identity crisis. This condition is manifest­ed by a loss of meaning in the profession, a decline in academic performance, and doubts about the validity of a career choice. Standardized criteria for the early detection of professional identity crisis, however, have not yet been established. Objective. To develop and validate a framework for screening for a professional identity crisis in medical university students using a set of psychological indicators. Materials and methods. The study involved 120 fourth through sixth-year students from the faculties of general medicine and pediatrics. The following instruments were used: the Purpose-in-Life Orientations Test (D.A. Leontiev), the Hardiness Scale by S. Maddi, the Ways of Coping Questionnaire by R. Lazarus, the method for studying learning motivation by T.I. Ilyina, and the author’s questionnaire for subjective assessment of the crisis. Statistical processing includ­ed comparative, cluster, and regression analyses. Results. Using cluster analysis and subsequent discriminant testing, three groups of students were identified: “successful” (30.8%), who do not experience crisis; “students experiencing crisis but having high personal resources for overcoming it” (38.3%), who maintain meaning in life, active coping and intrinsic motivation; and students (30.8%) whose subjective experience of crisis is combined with profound existential, emotional and behavioral disorders. Predictors of the maladaptive form of crisis were low meaning in life (в = -0.38), low level of resilience (control, в = -0.27), avoidance coping (в = 0.22) and lack of intrinsic motivation (в = -0.19), collectively explaining 71.4% of the variance. Conclusion. The developed screening tool help to early detect students in need of psychological support and to plan pre­ventive interventions on a case-by-vase basis.

items.title: From Algorithm Performance to Laboratory Deployment: A Critical Review of Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Chemistry
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied in clinical laboratories to support laboratory processes and interpretation of test results. Recent developments in machine learning, deep learning, and large language models have expanded the potential applications of AI across different stages of laboratory testing. However, the use of AI in clinical laboratories also raises important questions regarding validation, analytical performance, and transferability between laboratories. This narrative review examines recent applications of AI across the total testing process in clinical chemistry. Recent English-language scientific literature published from 2023 to 18 August 2026 was identified through searches of PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar. It describes AI-assisted test utilization; specimen handling and quality assessment; detection of laboratory errors; patient-based quality control; interpretation of complex analytical outputs, including signals from emerging AI-integrated biosensors and nanomaterial-based analytical platforms; result verification; and laboratory-report interpretation. The review also discusses major implementation challenges, including analytical variability, data quality, sensor and platform reproducibility, model generalizability, interoperability, and limitations of large language models. Particular attention is given to external validation, transportability, and real-world implementation. Among the studies considered in this review, many applications remain supported mainly by retrospective or internally validated studies, while prospective and operational evaluations are less common. Finally, practical considerations for validation, local verification, quality assurance, and performance monitoring are discussed. AI has considerable potential to support clinical chemistry laboratories, but safe use requires appropriate evaluation and continued involvement of laboratory professionals.

items.title: From Counting Cells to Reconstructing Death: A Commentary on Artificial Intelligence in Forensic Histopathology
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being investigated as a means to advance forensic histopathology from visual description to quantitative mapping, pattern recognition, and multimodal reconstruction of death. Recent developments in human postmortem analysis include validated whole-slide digitisation as foundational infrastructure and task-specific AI applications for diatom detection, glomerular quantification, coronary morphometry, myocardial classification, immunohistochemistry scoring, and virtual staining. AI-based postmortem interval (PMI) estimation remains experimental; the multi-organ study referenced in this commentary utilised an animal model, and human forensic validity has not yet been established. Foundation and vision-language models may ultimately extend these capabilities across organs and integrate microscopic findings with autopsy, toxicological, radiological, and circumstantial evidence. Postmortem tissue, however, is subject to autolysis, decomposition, agonal events, resuscitation, and non-standardised sampling, while the reference diagnosis is often a probabilistic whole-case opinion rather than an objective slide label. This work introduces FORENS-AI (FORensic Histopathology Evidence Network and Safeguards for AI), a conceptual architecture designed to convert computational outputs into traceable medicolegal evidence. FORENS-AI has not been empirically validated and is not presented as a standard, scoring system, clinical decision rule, or practice recommendation. The framework represents findings as an evidence graph, separates the Slide, Case, and Claim Gates, and proposes progressively stronger validation as outputs move from measurement to temporal, mechanistic, or causal inference. The primary aim is not to automate certification of death, but to identify safeguards to evaluate before AI-derived histological findings are permitted to inform expert opinion.

items.title: FROM DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION TO ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: A NEW PARADIGM OF GLOBAL JOURNALISM
items.abstract: The contemporary media industry is undergoing one of the most profound transformations in the history of mass communication. Digital platforms, social networks, mobile technologies, big data, algorithmic distribution systems and, most recently, generative artificial intelligence have fundamentally changed the production, distribution and consumption of information. The traditional model in which professional media institutions controlled the principal channels of information has evolved into a complex digital ecosystem where journalists, media organisations, technology platforms, bloggers, influencers, artificial intelligence systems and ordinary users simultaneously participate in the creation and circulation of content. This article examines the transformation of mass media in the context of digitalisation, technological innovation and the rapid development of artificial intelligence. Particular attention is paid to the integration of generative AI into newsroom processes, including information gathering, transcription, translation, data analysis, content production, fact-checking, personalisation and audience engagement. The study argues that artificial intelligence should not be interpreted merely as an instrument of automation. Rather, it represents a structural factor capable of changing journalistic workflows, professional competencies, editorial responsibility, media economics and the relationship between media institutions and their audiences. At the same time, AI-driven journalism generates significant professional and ethical risks, including algorithmic bias, hallucinated information, deepfakes, synthetic content, copyright disputes and the possible erosion of public trust. The article concludes that the future competitiveness and social legitimacy of media organisations will depend not simply on technological adoption, but on their ability to combine innovation with professional standards, human editorial oversight, transparency and accountability.

items.title: From Pattern to Interpretation: Topic Modeling as Editorial Record
items.abstract: Presentation at the 21st Annual Conference of the European Society for Textual Scholarship (ESTS 2026), Lublin, Poland. 30.05.2026. Abstract: Machine learning and artificial intelligence open new possibilities for dealing with large text corpora, where content structuring becomes essential because readers can no longer grasp the corpus through close reading alone. We think that approaches such as topic modeling or AI-based keyword assignment in digital editions can help address this challenge. Building on Hans Zeller’s foundational distinction between record (Befund) and interpretation (Deutung) (Zeller 1971), we argue that these computational approaches constitute a new layer of record. Although their analytical character may suggest an interpretive element, systematic and transparent documentation ensures that they do not exceed the interpretive scope inherent in any editorial practice (Martens 1994, S. 74; Sahle 2013, S. 210). Like qualitative editorial findings, this computational record may contain biases and opacities, which underscores the need for transparent documentation (Henny-Krahmer, Neuber 2014). Yet these methods could offer a curatorial angle, offering perspectives that can encourage editors to reassess their own biases and assumptions. By exposing patterns beyond the reach of close reading, they enhance the accessibility of the material and temporarily complement the editor’s work, offering additional interpretive pathways. Using the digital edition of Jean Paul's letters (Bernauer et al. 2018) as a case study (ca. 12,000 documents), we demonstrate how computational methods for content analysis can be integrated into editorial data models and interfaces. We will focus particularly on the interplay between computational findings (which remain record) and their interpretation (which requires human scholarly judgment); a relationship which we conceive as complementary rather than hierarchical.

items.title: From perception to practice: Faculty-led assessment redesign in response to generative AI in higher education
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT into higher education has unsettled long standing assumptions about the validity, reliability, and authenticity of conventional assessment methods. Existing research has predominantly examined perceptions, ethical concerns, and technology acceptance, leaving the actual pedagogical redesign work of faculty, and its relationship to established principles of assessment quality, comparatively underexplored. Drawing on constructive alignment theory, this study examines how faculty are reshaping assessment design under conditions of AI disruption and whether their adaptation strategies address or fail to address core dimensions of assessment validity. A sequential explanatory mixed methods design was used across two phases: a survey of 180 faculty members across STEM and non STEM disciplines at a private institution in India, followed by semi structured interviews and assessment artefact analysis with a purposively selected subset of participants. The results show a marked shift away from unsupervised, product based assessment toward process oriented, reflective, and authentic formats, including oral examinations, project based tasks, in class problem solving, and reflective journals, an implicit faculty led re alignment of assessment with intended learning outcomes. Faculty frame GenAI simultaneously as a threat to assessment integrity and as a catalyst for pedagogical innovation, but institutional structures have not kept pace with this bottom up change, and increased workload, inconsistent guidance, and limited professional development persist as barriers to sustaining and scaling redesign. By empirically documenting faculty led transformation and connecting it explicitly to theories of assessment quality and institutional change, the study moves beyond descriptive accounts of GenAI's impact and offers practical guidance for educators, instructional designers, and institutional leaders seeking to formalise sustainable, valid, and equitable assessment redesign in the GenAI era.

items.title: From Stages to States: Unified Iterative Reasoning for MLLMs
items.abstract: Multimodal Chain-of-Thought (MCoT) substantially enhances the complex reasoning capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by explicitly modeling intermediate reasoning processes. However, most learning-based MCoT methods follow a stage-centric paradigm, where different reasoning behaviors are assigned to predefined stages and optimized separately. This results in fragmented reasoning and a training-inference reasoning-state gap. To address these limitations, we propose ReState, a unified iterative reasoning framework that reformulates multimodal reasoning from a stage-driven pipeline into a state-driven dynamic process. It comprises two complementary components: Unified Reasoning State Modeling (URSM) and Closed-Loop Reasoning-State Learning (CRSL). URSM unifies reasoning construction, correct reasoning preservation, and erroneous reasoning correction as reasoning-state transitions within a shared state space, enabling these heterogeneous reasoning behaviors to be learned jointly. CRSL further incorporates self-generated historical reasoning states during training and recursively updates the current state during inference, thereby mitigating the reasoning-state gap and enabling iterative self-refinement without requiring an additional reflection module, critic, or independent correction stage. Furthermore, we construct VersaCoT-10K, a high-quality CoT dataset spanning eight visual reasoning domains, which provides diverse supervision for multi-domain reasoning and reasoning-state refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReState exhibits strong adaptability across different MLLM backbones and achieves strong performance on multiple public reasoning benchmarks, supporting the shift from stage-centric reasoning toward state-centric reasoning. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/YuChuang1205/ReState

items.title: GaCLLM: Large Language Model with Graph Convolution for Recommendation
items.abstract: Leveraging auxiliary textual data can help with user profiling and item characterization in recommender systems (RSs). However, incomplete user and item descriptions limit the potential of textual information. To this end, we propose a graph-aware convolutional large language model (LLM) method, eliciting LLMs to summarize from a high-order interaction graph to generate fine-grained descriptions for users and items. We focus on two challenges in this paper: 1) the incompatibility between structural graph and text-aware LLMs . Although some work converts graph data into textual form using templates and sampling strategies, they limit the LLMs’ ability to maintain a global perspective on graphs for LLM reasoning. 2) the limitation of LLMs’ capability for long context. Simply describing a large-scale graph in a textual format makes LLM struggle to robustly comprehend information from lengthy contextual inputs. To bridge the gap between graph structures and LLMs, we employ the LLM as an aggregator for the graph convolution process, eliciting it to aggregate and refine the graph-based information iteratively. To mitigate the information overload associated with large-scale graphs, we segment the graph processing into manageable steps, progressively incorporating multi-hop information in a least-to-most manner. Experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches.

items.title: Generalizable Model Editing Could Be More Than Direct Generalization
items.abstract: A central desideratum in model editing is generalization to complex tasks, which prior work formalizes under a direct generalization paradigm: treating and evaluating LLM behavior as an input-output mapping and expecting a factual update to alter outputs on reasoning tasks. Yet despite substantial empirical effort, the field consensus remains that such generalization is highly challenging and elusive. However, when we deploy the latest models in an in-the-wild chatbot-user setting, we surprisingly find that even classical editing methods exhibit remarkably fluent generalization behavior. This motivates us to revisit the obstacles to generalization and the limitations of the prevailing paradigm. We find that direct generalization is fundamentally constrained both theoretically and practically: theoretically, it suffers from an identifiability issue; and practically, existing approaches attempting to circumvent this are further hindered by the ambiguity of their constructed biases and by vulnerability to being overridden by other factors such as optimization dynamics. We instead identify compositional generalization, empowered by the increasingly strong reasoning and composition abilities of modern LLMs, as a theoretically grounded and empirically validated alternative. We validate this phenomenon across multiple models and editing methods, showing that such generalization behavior is widespread. Overall, we argue that generalizable model editing could be more than direct generalization, and call for a paradigm shift toward more generalizable and practically deployable knowledge update techniques.

items.title: Generative AI enables human-centered design of sustainable plant-based foods
items.abstract: Dietary transitions away from animal-based meat could reduce food-related environmental burdens, but plant-based alternatives must compete on flavor, texture, and overall liking. Here we extend a generative AI framework with 469 plant-based burger recipes and use it to create six formulations across five primary ingredients: bean, chickpea, lentil, mushroom, and oat. An executive chef translates the AI-generated formulations into standardized preparation protocols and refines the ingredient quantities based on culinary expertise. The integration of generative modeling and culinary expertise defines a human-centered generative AI framework for food design. We evaluate the six burgers in a blinded sensory survey with 101 participants in an operating restaurant and quantify their land use, greenhouse gas emissions, eutrophication potential, and scarcity-weighted water use. We use Big Mac scores from a previous survey as an iconic commercial benchmark. The mushroom burger achieves mean flavor, texture, and overall liking scores similar to the Big Mac, with less than one-third of its estimated environmental impact. The other formulations reduce the estimated impact further, in several cases to near one-tenth of the Big Mac value, but receive lower liking scores. Mixed-effects models quantify associations between sensory attributes and human liking and retain predictive accuracy on independent survey data, with mean absolute errors no greater than 0.52 points on a seven-point scale. Together, these results demonstrate how generative design, culinary expertise, human sensory response, and environmental assessment can converge to create sustainable foods that people want to eat.

items.title: Generative AI Feedback and Learning Engagement in Distributed Learning Environments: The Roles of Feedback Literacy and Self-Regulated Learning
items.abstract: Distributed learning environments address the constraints of fixed locations and schedules in traditional education, offering diverse teaching approaches, including online, blended, and lifelong learning. Learners can make the most of fragmented learning opportunities by engaging in a range of learning activities. At the same time, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers real-time interaction, personalized adaptation, and dynamic learning opportunities, potentially creating more flexible learning pathways in distributed learning environments. AI-generated feedback may also support learners' engagement in the learning process. Feedback literacy and self-regulated learning may play important roles in supporting learners' sustained engagement. This paper explores how feedback literacy and self-regulated learning may shape the relationship between generative AI feedback and learner engagement in distributed learning environments. It also proposes an integrated educational framework that combines AI-enhanced feedback, competency development, and instructional monitoring and support to promote sustained learning engagement.

items.title: Generative AI Literacy and Multidimensional AI Anxiety in Creative Higher Education
items.abstract: Engagement with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) involves practical literacy as well as learning, professional, sociotechnical, and configuration concerns. This mixed-methods study examined whether these responses were differentiated among Chinese arts-university students. Primary inference used a quality-screened cross-sectional sample of 355 questionnaire records from 351 participant-identifier clusters after excluding 105 of 460 eligible records (22.8%) showing exact whole-battery straightlining across all 59 structured items; the full eligible sample of 460 records from 455 clusters was retained as a sensitivity analysis. GenAI literacy was assessed with a 16-item music-context-adapted self-report instrument covering cognitive (CL), behavioral (BL), affective (AL), and ethical (EL) literacy, and AI Anxiety with 21 items spanning Learning Anxiety (LA), Job-Replacement Anxiety (JR), Sociotechnical Blindness Anxiety (ST), and AI Configuration Anxiety (AC). Of six prespecified associations, only EL-JR and EL-ST met the Holm-adjusted criterion in the primary sample and remained supported in the full-sample and prior-use-adjusted sensitivity analyses. CL-LA and BL-LA were unsupported in both samples, whereas AL-LA and AL-AC were sample-specification sensitive. Measurement models showed mixed fit; CL-BL separation improved after quality screening but remained incomplete. A secondary 47-person exact-identifier matched panel showed higher later-wave CL, BL, and AL scores, whereas EL and all four AI Anxiety dimensions showed no Holm-adjusted difference. These literacy comparisons are exploratory because the administered literacy items were music-framed while the documented learning activities involved broadcasting scripts and AI-supported video production. Independently analyzed qualitative material provided construct-level consistency with the EL-ST interpretation and tentative complementarity for EL-JR, but was not participant-linked to the quantitative samples. Overall, the evidence supports a bounded interpretation of differentiated, calibrated rather than anxiety-free adaptation; it does not establish causal intervention effects or participant-level mixed-method mechanisms.

items.title: Genesis: Visual Augmentation Primitives for Multimodal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
items.abstract: Recent multimodal large language models achieve promising results on visual reasoning tasks, approaching human-level performance on existing STEM benchmarks. However, these capabilities degrade under complex real-world scenes. We identify that chain-of-thought reasoning remains largely confined to the linguistic space, rarely anchoring each step in visual evidence. The main cause is the absence of such data during training. In this work, we introduce a training data augmentation pipeline, \textbf{Visual Augmentation Primitives} (VAP), which leverages state-of-the-art vision generative models to synthesize diverse photorealistic training samples and corresponding reasoning text. VAP introduces some basic operators and applies them to a seed image and gets a variant. It also constructs coherent multimodal reasoning chains throughout the generation process. Such training data force models to perceive visual content and perform logical reasoning according to them at every step. We further introduce multimodal chain-of-thought rubric-based reinforcement learning to enhance this. It rewards not only text reasoning but also visual reasoning by scoring intermediate reasoning steps for logical validity, completeness, and consistency. Moreover, we construct the UNREAL benchmark to systematically evaluate visual reasoning on hyperrealistic scenes across controllable difficulty levels. Experiments show that a 4B model built on this framework surpasses 8B baselines, with performance improving consistently as the model scales to 32B, validating the scaling law for visual reasoning.

items.title: Google Earth AI Geospatial Reasoning Agent: Capabilities and a Systematic Evaluation
items.abstract: Google Earth AI is a family of geospatial AI models, together with an agent that orchestrates them. We present this agent, Google Earth AI's Geospatial Reasoning agent (GRA), a Gemini-powered research system that combines geospatial data sources, foundation models, and tools to answer questions about our planet. GRA organizes these into modular domain skills and pairs them with upfront geospatial planning to decompose complex queries into multi-stage workflows. Evaluating such systems is hard: real-world problems admit multiple valid workflows, require data discovery across large catalogs, and rely on evolving ground truth. We introduce two benchmarks and release their development splits. GeoExpertQueries poses complex analytical problems grounded in practitioner use cases and refined by geospatial experts; each is paired with a consensus golden workflow from three independent experts and scored by a human-validated, tool-agnostic autorater. GeoKTools consists of templated queries with deterministic reference solvers that systematically vary the number of required tool types. We also use two external benchmarks, CBGB and UnivEARTH; the latter we find to be saturated. To isolate the contribution of GRA's tools and its agentic orchestration, we compare four configurations, each with Gemini 3.1 Pro and 3.8 Flash: a standalone LLM, the LLM with basic tools, the LLM with GRA's skills and tools but without its upfront planning and execution guidance, and GRA itself. With at most basic tools, an advanced model recovers much of the answer on templated queries but satisfies only a small fraction of the expert workflows on open-ended problems; GRA performs well on both. The largest step comes from GRA's skills and tools; on open-ended problems, its planning and execution guidance add a further gain with Gemini 3.8 Flash, letting Flash match or exceed Pro at lower cost.

items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is becoming routine in university study, yet institutional responses often separate technical fluency, academic integrity, and responsible governance. This integrative conceptual synthesis develops governance-aware GenAI literacy for adult higher education. A bounded, purposive review of 28 sources published through 10 September 2026 combined peer-reviewed studies, foundational scholarship, policy frameworks, and one preprint. Sources were coded for learning capability, epistemic risk, pedagogical mechanism, governance requirement, and strength of evidence. The resulting framework comprises five connected domains: epistemic verification, task and interaction specification, dialogic reflection, ethical governance, and transfer to professional action, all centred on visible human accountability. The framework extends beyond text prompting to multimodal, personalised, and agentic systems. It is translated into a pilot-ready eight-week sequence, tiered workload model, assessment evidence, accessibility safeguards, disciplinary adaptations, and an evaluation protocol. The paper does not claim empirical validation of the model or optimality of the sequence. Instead, it offers a bounded design proposition for testing. Governance-aware literacy is presented as the capacity to use AI productively while documenting, verifying, contesting, and justifying its contribution in academic and professional contexts.

items.title: GroundSTory: Interactive Storytelling for Grounded Spatiotemporal Anomaly Explanations with Graphs and Large Language Models
items.abstract: Explaining anomalies in spatiotemporal data requires more than identifying statistical deviations; it often demands coherent narratives that relate events to their spatial, temporal, and social context. In urban settings, where anomalies may reflect public events, behavioral shifts, or environmental factors, the lack of interpretable, contextual explanations limits the effectiveness of automated analysis. We present GroundSTory , an interactive framework that reframes spatiotemporal anomaly explanation as computational storytelling, integrating graph-based representations of urban space, coordinated visual analytics, and large language models (LLMs) to support the construction of grounded, human-readable narrative explanations. Anomalies act as narrative anchors, while localized spatial and temporal relations and contextual signals derived from the graph guide and constrain narrative generation. The LLM functions as a narrative assistant, proposing plausible, evidence-backed hypotheses that analysts can inspect, compare, and validate through visual interaction. We illustrate the approach through qualitative usage scenarios on real-world urban datasets from São Paulo and New York City, showing how interactive narratives surface meaningful links between detected anomalies and contextual factors such as holidays, mass events, and routine activity patterns. A prompt analysis further suggests that structured, graph-derived context tends to affect the stability and perceived quality of generated hypotheses. Overall, our results indicate that combining knowledge-driven representations, interactive visualization, and constrained prompting can support more coherent, plausible, and interpretable narratives for spatiotemporal anomaly analysis, contributing to ongoing research in interactive storytelling and narrative-centered AI systems.

items.title: Hand2Robot: Object-Centric 4D Hand Reconstruction from Human Demonstrations for Robotics
items.abstract: Human demonstrations can capture task-relevant manipulation without using the target robot, but the recorded hand motions cannot directly serve as robot action supervision. Hand reconstruction and motion retargeting provide a direct route to such supervision, yet recovering hand motion alone does not ensure physically consistent hand-object interactions. To address this issue, we introduce Hand2Robot, an object-centric 4D hand reconstruction framework for robot policy post-training. Given videos of humans performing the target task, Hand2Robot extracts interaction clips, reconstructs object geometry, and generates robot action supervision through hand-object interaction optimization and motion retargeting. For object tracking, we combine observation confidence with temporal motion constraints to select a globally consistent object pose trajectory from per-frame pose candidates. For hand refinement, we use object geometry and motion as a reference and combine staged 2D alignment with object-local contact constraints to refine hand trajectories and finger joint configurations. Experiments on DexYCB and HO3D-v3 show improved object pose accuracy and hand-object interaction quality. Experiments on three real-robot dexterous manipulation tasks further show that reconstructed and retargeted human demonstrations can effectively supplement limited robot data for target-task policy post-training.

items.title: Harnessing AI for Sustainable Finance: Current Applications and Future Horizons
items.abstract: Purpose: This chapter looks at how artificial intelligence (AI) can enable sustainable financial activities, especially in terms of risk assessment, optimisation of investment, and compliance with regulation to promote healthy, inclusive financial systems. Need for the study: Finance and sustainable finance are reshaping the world markets as the sustainability issues of the environment, social, and governance (ESG) increase, but the difficulties of data biases, ethical issues, and regulatory uncertainties remain. AI integration applies to these by improving ESG ratings, climate risk analysis, and impact investments and growing the industry to $2.5 trillion. Methodology: The review of AI-based technologies, including machine learning (ML), natural language processing (NLP), and big data analytics, is conducted and reviewed in the context of their use in the ESG scoring, carbon footprint estimation, and predictive climate forecasting based on the case studies of the global financial institutions. Findings: AI generates better financial returns in ESG portfolios compared to traditional ones, enhances transparency in sustainability, reduces fraud, and allows accurate predictive instruments on climate event risks to support green bond strategies. Practical implications: Researchers of AI and policymakers, as well as institutions, should cooperate in order to limit bias and ethical concerns, enabling equitable adoption of AI to support sustainable robust finance.

items.title: Healthcare Professionals’ Perspectives on Agentic Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Work: A Qualitative Study
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into healthcare, primarily supporting clinical decision-making. Agentic AI may extend these applications by autonomously planning, coordinating, and executing clinical and administrative workflows. However, empirical evidence on how healthcare professionals conceptualise agentic AI and anticipate its implications for work and occupational well-being remains limited. This study explores healthcare professionals’ perceptions and expectations regarding agentic AI and its potential effects on healthcare work. Methods: We conducted a qualitative study using semi-structured interviews with 25 healthcare professionals from different clinical backgrounds in Germany. Interviews explored perceptions of agentic AI, focusing on workflow organisation, workload, professional autonomy, accountability, and occupational well-being. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke. Results: Five themes were identified: (1) from assisting decisions to organising work; (2) automation redistributes rather than removes work; (3) delegating action without delegating responsibility; (4) implications for working conditions and health- and work-related outcomes; and (5) meaningful human control requires organisational conditions. Participants distinguished between conventional AI-based decision support and more autonomous forms of AI in their accounts, using this contrast to describe potential changes in workflow organisation. Their accounts highlighted practical consequences of delegating workflow-related activities to AI systems, including changes in task structures, monitoring and verification demands, exception management, and the distribution of professional responsibility. Participants anticipated reduced routine administrative workload and improved care coordination, but also potential increases in cognitive and supervisory demands. Conclusions: Agentic AI may shift healthcare from AI-assisted decision-making towards AI-mediated workflow execution. Its effects on occupational well-being may therefore be bidirectional, combining workload relief with increased cognitive and supervisory demands. Appropriate governance, clearly defined accountability, meaningful human oversight, workforce training, and regulatory alignment will be essential for responsible implementation.

items.title: Hearts for hating Activists: how far-right actors dominate polarized TikTok debates on climate protest
items.abstract: This study investigates degrees of polarization in political climate protest debates on TikTok. Drawing on a dataset of automatically transcribed TikTok videos posted by German politicians between 2022 and 2025 (N ≈ 1,700), alongside associated user comments (N ≈ 53,000), this study compares discussions on general climate activism, reformist activism (Fridays for Future), and disruptive activism (Letzte Generation). Using a mixed-method approach that combines Large Language Model-based frame classification, stance detection, and network analysis, this study operationalizes Discursive Polarization across ideological, affective, and interactional dimensions. Findings reveal that while all protest debates on TikTok are polarized, disruptive protests are associated with particularly intense attacks and less attention to policy-oriented climate discussions. However, conservative and far-right politicians consistently frame all activist groups as extremists, criminals, or threats to public order, with far-right accounts dominating content production and audience support. Network analyses demonstrate that far-right politicians and their supporters form highly connected clusters in which both emotionally positive and hostile user engagement amplifies elite-level antagonism. Even moderate posts by center-left or progressive politicians attract disproportionate backlash, suggesting asymmetric polarization dynamics linked to partisan user networks. Overall, the study shows that political TikTok debates around climate protest are consistently polarized along ideological lines, but that greater disruptiveness coincides with more intense antagonistic engagement and weaker Connective Action among supporters. Most crucially, far-right politicians emerge as the clear beneficiaries of this polarization, occupying central positions in antagonist networks of Connective Counteraction and dominating the debate through disruption.

items.title: Hidden in Plain Sight: Advancing Harmful Content Understanding via Perception-Aware Adversarial Self-Play
items.abstract: Despite significant advances in language understanding, Large Language Models (LLMs) can still miss meaning hidden in plain sight, failing to identify harmful intent in expressions readily understood by humans. Malicious users exploit this gap by strategically disguising harmful content to evade automated moderation, posing a serious threat to online platform safety. The vulnerability reflects a fundamental cognitive asymmetry between human readers, who integrate contextual, phonetic, and visual cues to decipher the intent behind deliberate obfuscation, and text-based LLMs, which rely primarily on token sequences and have limited exposure to evolving evasions. To bridge this asymmetry, we propose PASP (Perception-Aware Adversarial Self-Play), which combines multi-perceptual views with adversarial self-play to improve understanding of harmful intent as evasions evolve. Specifically, PASP constructs textual, phonetic, and visual views of each input, preserving its original context while exposing pronunciation and glyph cues obscured in token space. During adversarial self-play, an attacker uses defender feedback to generate intent-preserving evasions, while the defender is trained using an intent-invariance reward to understand harmful intent across changing surface forms. Extensive experiments show that PASP reduces adaptive attack success rates by up to 73.71% and 74.49% on ChineseHarm-Bench and EvoHarmBench, respectively, preserves model capabilities with minimal degradation, and effectively interprets real-world evasive expressions in e-commerce.
